name: Hitchens's Razor
statement: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.
meaning: Hitchens's razor is the epistemic rule that a claim offered with no evidence may be rejected with no evidence. The burden of proof lies with the person making the claim; if they do not meet it, others are entitled to set the claim aside without having to argue against it. It is a restatement of an old maxim about who owes the argument.
mechanism: The razor works by placing the burden of proof squarely on the claimant. To assert something is not to establish it, so an unsupported assertion earns no standing and can be waved away without counter-argument. This licenses dismissal, not disproof: it does not show the claim false, only that, absent evidence, no one is obliged to take it seriously. It is a rule about the economy of argument — who must do the work — rather than about truth itself.

examples.text: Hitchens deployed the razor against unevidenced theological assertions, its original use in his book against religion.
A claim of a miracle cure or a hidden plot, offered without supporting evidence, can be dismissed on the same ground, the burden resting on whoever asserts it.
Bertrand Russell's image of an unfalsifiable teapot orbiting the Sun makes the same point: the burden of disproof does not fall on the sceptic.

variants.name: The Latin antecedent
variants.text: The centuries-old maxim that what is asserted gratuitously may be denied gratuitously, documented in use well before Hitchens, with an early instance by the theologian Pritius in 1704.

variants.name: The Sagan standard
variants.text: The related principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, likewise placing the evidential onus on the one making the claim.

whyItMatters: It is a compact, memorable statement of the burden of proof, widely invoked in debates over religion, pseudoscience, and conspiracy theories to insist that the one making a claim must support it. As a rhetorical tool it keeps argument honest by refusing to let unsupported assertions shift the work of disproof onto the sceptic.

working.lead: Put the burden on the claimant
working.text: require whoever makes a claim to supply the evidence, rather than demanding others disprove it.
set aside an unsupported claim without argument, while remembering this shows only that it lacks standing, not that it is false.
hold your own assertions to the same standard, offering evidence rather than expecting them to be granted.

limits: It is a rhetorical and epistemic heuristic, not a formal law of logic. Critics argue it can be corrosive to reasoned discourse by prematurely shutting down discussion, and reformed epistemologists hold that some basic beliefs can be rational without propositional evidence, challenging its premise. Crucially, it concerns the burden of proof, not truth: dismissing an unsupported claim does not establish that the claim is false, only that no one is obliged to accept it. And what counts as evidence, or enough of it, can itself be contested.
misreadings: Hitchens did not originate the principle; he popularised it, and it is centuries older, traceable to a Latin maxim and to a 1704 use by Pritius. The name Hitchens's razor was applied by others after his book, not coined by him. And the razor does not prove the opposing claim false — it enforces the burden of proof and licenses dismissal, not disproof.
origin: Popularised by the writer Christopher Hitchens in 'God Is Not Great' (2007) and named after him by others around 2011; it restates the older maxim that what is asserted without evidence may be denied without evidence.

sources.text: Hitchens's razor, Wikipedia. — the statement, its appearance in God Is Not Great, the naming after Hitchens, and the Latin antecedent.
Reinhardt, "The long history of Hitchens' Razor," Skeptic Ink (2015). — the older provenance and the 1704 Pritius use.
